---
title: "Research"
---

I am interested in how cells decide when, where and how strongly to express their
genes, with a focus on plants. Most of my work is about transcription: how
regulatory DNA and chromatin determine where it begins and how much of it occurs,
and how this changes during development and in response to the environment. I
combine genome-wide assays and genetics with computational models of regulatory
sequence, and earlier in my career I applied comparative genomics to bacterial
pathogens.

## Transcription initiation and non-coding transcription

Much of what a promoter does is visible only at the level of transcription start
sites. Using csRNA-seq, which captures nascent initiation events directly, I showed
that divergent and non-coding transcription is an active part of gene regulation
during the *Arabidopsis* seed-to-seedling transition, and validated these events
genetically
([Nature Communications, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46082-5)).

## Gene regulation in a changing environment

Plants in the field experience fluctuating temperature, light and pathogens. I led
the bioinformatics for a multi-laboratory study of how *Arabidopsis* transcription
changes as autumn progresses into winter under simulated field temperatures
([Genome Biology, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-026-04289-3)). At The
Sainsbury Laboratory I am combining csRNA-seq with single-nucleus RNA and ATAC
multiomics to connect immune-responsive transcription to candidate enhancers and to
resolve how individual cell types respond to infection (posters from
[2025](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21476383) and
[2026](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21476601)). I am also taking these
approaches beyond plants: with collaborators, I am profiling transcription
initiation in the algal and fungal partners of lichens, building on our work on
transposable element diversification in lichen symbionts
([bioRxiv, 2026](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.02.14.705750)).

![*Arabidopsis* plants moved from 22 °C into constant, gradually cooling or fluctuating
temperature regimes that follow autumn field temperatures recorded in Sweden. From
Ormancey, Tremblay, Cheng et al. (2026), *Genome Biology*, Fig. 1A–C
([CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)).](images/research/seasons.png){width=65% fig-align="center" fig-alt="Experimental design, temperature profiles and photos of Arabidopsis plants in three temperature regimes"}

## Sulfur metabolism and plant development

My MSc work asked what happens when plants cannot efficiently recycle
methylthioadenosine (MTA), a by-product of polyamine, nicotianamine and ethylene
synthesis. MTA
builds up mainly in reproductive tissues, where it disrupts sulfur assimilation and
lowers the methyl index, with knock-on effects on gene expression and DNA
methylation that reduce fertility
([Journal of Experimental Botany, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1093/jxb/erag135)).

![The sulfur assimilation pathway, SAM cycle and methionine salvage, showing where
MTA is produced during the synthesis of polyamines (Spd, Spm, Tspm), nicotianamine
(NA) and ethylene (Eth). From Tremblay et al. (2026), *Journal of Experimental
Botany*, Fig. 3A
([CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)).](images/research/sulfur.png){width=40% fig-align="center" fig-alt="Diagram of sulfur assimilation, the SAM cycle and methionine salvage"}

## Models of regulatory sequence

I train and interpret deep sequence-to-function models of chromatin accessibility
and transcription initiation, and use them to ask which sequence features explain
regulatory activity. This builds on my long-running work on sequence motifs and the
[universalmotif](software.qmd) package.

![A contribution-weight logo of a CACGTG motif, in which bases can contribute
positively or negatively, drawn with universalmotif.](images/research/motif.png){fig-alt="Sequence logo with positive and negative base contributions around a CACGTG motif"}

## Microbial genomics

Between my MSc and PhD I worked on the comparative genomics of bacterial pathogens,
including the phylogenomics of 8,839 *Clostridioides difficile* genomes
([PLOS Pathogens, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1009181)) and
phylogenetic profiling of bacterial gene function
([Bioinformatics, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa1105)). I also
contributed to studies identifying TFPI as a receptor for *C. difficile* toxin B
variants ([Nature Communications, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-33964-9))
and recovering tetanus neurotoxin variants from ancient DNA
([Nature Communications, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41174-0)).

## SARS-CoV-2 and the human airway

During the COVID-19 pandemic I worked with clinicians and virologists on SARS-CoV-2, predicting its recombination potential ([Journal of General Virology, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1099/jgv.0.001491)) and profiling viral receptors and interferon responses in human airway epithelium ([European Respiratory Journal, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.01123-2020); [iScience, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2021.102477)).
